lisbon.title: The 1972 Managua earthquake
lisbon.line: A quake killed thousands in Nicaragua’s capital, and claims that Somoza’s circle pocketed foreign aid fed the revolt that toppled him.

lisbon.title: The 1976 Tangshan earthquake
lisbon.line: Officially 242,000 died, the toll stayed hidden for three years, and Mao’s death weeks later made the quake look like an omen.

lisbon.title: The 1985 Mexico City earthquake
lisbon.line: As thousands died and the government stalled, volunteers dug out survivors themselves, and anger over shoddy buildings weakened the ruling PRI.

lisbon.title: The 2008 Sichuan earthquake
lisbon.line: Over 69,000 died, including thousands of pupils in poorly built “tofu-dreg” schools, and grieving parents who demanded answers faced police pressure.

revolution.title: Peasant rebels topple the Ming dynasty
revolution.line: After years of famine and a court mired in factions, Li Zicheng’s rebels took Beijing, and the last Ming emperor hanged himself.

revolution.title: Russia’s February Revolution
revolution.line: Bread protests by Petrograd women grew into strikes and army mutinies, and within a week Tsar Nicholas II abdicated.

revolution.title: Indonesia’s 1998 revolt topples Suharto
revolution.line: As the Asian financial crisis sent food and fuel prices soaring, protests and riots ended Suharto’s 32-year rule, criticised for cronyism.

hamilton.title: United Italy merges its states’ debts
hamilton.line: The new Kingdom of Italy gathered the debts of the old states it absorbed into a single national ledger, the Gran Libro.

hamilton.title: Canadian Confederation takes on provincial debts
hamilton.line: At Confederation, the new Dominion of Canada took on the debts of its provinces, a key bargain in uniting them.

vaccine.title: Boston’s smallpox inoculation fight
vaccine.line: Cotton Mather and Zabdiel Boylston promoted inoculation during an epidemic, and the backlash was fierce: someone threw a bomb into Mather’s house.

vaccine.title: Rio de Janeiro’s Vaccine Revolt
vaccine.line: A law making smallpox vaccination compulsory sparked a week of riots in Rio, leaving about 30 dead before the mandate was suspended.

vaccine.title: Salk’s polio vaccine and the Cutter incident
vaccine.line: Weeks after Jonas Salk’s polio vaccine was declared safe, faulty Cutter batches with live virus caused paralysis and ten deaths, shaking trust.

luddites.title: London weavers riot against engine looms
luddites.line: London silk weavers rioted for days, smashing and burning the engine looms they feared would undercut their pay and jobs.

luddites.title: The Swing Riots
luddites.line: Farm labourers across southern England smashed threshing machines that took their winter work, sending threats signed “Captain Swing”; 19 were hanged.

luddites.title: The Wapping print dispute
luddites.line: Rupert Murdoch’s papers moved to a computerised plant at Wapping; about 6,000 print workers struck, were dismissed, and lost after a year.

railway.title: The first passenger elevator opens
railway.line: Elisha Otis, whose safety brake eased fears of falling, installed the first passenger elevator in a New York store.

railway.title: A flying boat starts scheduled airline service
railway.line: The St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line flew paying passengers across Tampa Bay; the first ticket, auctioned off, went to an ex-mayor for $400.

railway.title: The first jet airliner enters service
railway.line: BOAC’s Comet began the first jet passenger flights, but two mid-air breakups in 1954, traced to metal fatigue, grounded the fleet.

mania.title: Britain’s canal mania
mania.line: Investors piled into canal schemes, and Parliament approved dozens in a few years; some never paid a dividend or were never finished.

mania.title: America’s railroad boom ends in panic
mania.line: After 33,000 miles of new track in five years, Jay Cooke’s bank failed with unsold Northern Pacific bonds, setting off a depression.

mania.title: The fibre-optic telecom bust
mania.line: Telecom firms borrowed to lay fibre-optic cable far beyond demand; when the bubble burst, much sat unused and Global Crossing went bankrupt.

springtime.title: The revolutions of 1830
springtime.line: France’s July Revolution toppled Charles X, and within months revolts broke out in Belgium, which won independence, and in Russian-ruled Poland.

springtime.title: The global protests of 1968
springtime.line: Protests swept Paris, West Germany, Mexico City and US campuses within months, as students worldwide shared slogans and television images.

springtime.title: The fall of communism in Eastern Europe
springtime.line: Within months, communist governments fell in Poland, Hungary, East Germany, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia and Romania, each crowd inspired by the last.

springtime.title: The Arab Spring
springtime.line: After Tunisia’s ruler fled, protests leapt within weeks to Egypt, Libya, Yemen, Bahrain and Syria, spread by satellite TV and social media.

cable.title: Marconi’s radio signal crosses the Atlantic
cable.line: Guglielmo Marconi reported hearing the Morse letter “S” in Newfoundland, sent by radio from Cornwall, showing signals could cross oceans without wires.

cable.title: The first transatlantic telephone cable opens
cable.line: TAT-1 linked Scotland and Newfoundland, carrying 707 calls on its first day, far clearer than the old radio telephone service.

cable.title: Telstar beams live TV across the Atlantic
cable.line: The Telstar satellite relayed the first live TV across the Atlantic, and like the 1858 cable, it failed within months.

carrington.title: The 1921 New York Railroad Storm
carrington.line: Storm currents set a Swedish telegraph exchange and New York railroad signal equipment ablaze, and disrupted telegraphs on several continents.

carrington.title: The August 1972 solar storm
carrington.line: A fast solar storm knocked out a Midwest phone cable and likely set off dozens of US sea mines off Vietnam.

carrington.title: Solar storm blacks out Quebec
carrington.line: A geomagnetic storm collapsed Hydro-Québec’s grid in under 90 seconds, leaving millions in Quebec without power for about nine hours.

carrington.title: The 2003 Halloween solar storms
carrington.line: Solar storms blacked out part of southern Sweden for an hour, forced satellites into safe mode and rerouted polar flights.

commune.title: Étienne Marcel’s revolt in Paris
commune.line: After the king’s capture by the English, Paris merchant leader Étienne Marcel defied the Dauphin’s government and briefly controlled the capital.

commune.title: Brittany’s Bonnets Rouges revolt
commune.line: Breton peasants in red caps rose against Louis XIV’s new taxes on stamped paper, tobacco and tin goods, and were harshly crushed.

commune.title: The revolt of the Languedoc winegrowers
commune.line: As wine prices collapsed, up to 800,000 rallied in Montpellier, local officials resigned en masse, and Clemenceau sent troops.

commune.title: Brittany’s red caps return
commune.line: Bretons in red caps recalling 1675 wrecked gantries built to collect a new truck ecotax, and the government suspended the tax.

phone.title: The first handheld mobile phone call
phone.line: On a Manhattan sidewalk, Motorola’s Martin Cooper called a rival at AT&T’s Bell Labs on a brick-sized prototype, starting the mobile age.
